text.p: Contract negotiations between American Airlines and its pilots continued throughout the weekend but both sides declined to comment on the progress of the talks.
"Talks are still ongoing at this moment as far as we know," Jim Philpot, a pilots' union spokesman, said late on Sunday.

The Presidential Emergency Board (PEB) was expected to submit a proposed settlement to President Clinton on Monday. The pilots' union said the PEB had not indicated when its report would be made public.
The White House convened the PEB on February 15 to try to resolve the dispute between the nation's second largest airline and its 9,300 pilots.
The president of the Allied Pilots Association earlier said the union and American Airlines would try to reach an agreement before the PEB submitted its report to Clinton.

The pilots' union said they would not make any additional comments about the progress of the talks until Monday. The union said its board plans to meet in Washington March 21 and March 22 to discuss the PEB's proposed settlement.
American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp, also declined to comment on Sunday on the weekend session.
"The PEB has indicated it wants everyone to refrain from commenting," a spokeswoman for the airline said.
The pilots and American met throughout the weekend at an undisclosed location. The meeting was the first time in a month the two sides had resumed contract negotiations.
Last month, both sides were outspoken, holding several press conferences during a week of fruitless negotiations that ended in a brief pilot's strike on February 15.
Clinton's decision to convene the emergency board meant the pilots had to return to their jobs for 60 days.
During the first 30 days, the board was to gather information and make proposals for an agreement. The pilots then have another 30 days to decide whether to accept the agreement.

If they reject it, they are free to strike again, although Congress can pass a law to force them to return to work and accept the board's proposed contract or to go into binding arbitration with the airline.
One issue in dispute is wages. Pilots are seeking an 11 percent pay raise to cover the past three years when there were no raises and the next four years. American offered 6.6 percent.

At issue also is whether the union's pilots, who earn an average of $120,000 a year, will fly new, small commuter jets American is to buy for its regional airline American Eagle, or whether they will be flown by Eagle pilots, who earn much less.
American has said it needed lower-paid pilots in order to be competitive with its rivals who are operating low-cost commuter jet services. The union wants its pilots to be in the cockpit.
